datapoints.value_text: MLX 4-bit: ~18-20 tok/s (some tests 20-28 depending on context); LM Studio/llama.cpp Q4: 11.8 tok/s (measured). ~40-43GB memory in Q4.
datapoints.source_name: siliconscore M4 Max 128GB page (measured, LM Studio Q4=11.8) + Sean Kim / imseankim M4 Max inference benchmarks (MLX ~20)
datapoints.notes: WIDE framework spread. siliconscore aggregates external community benchmarks: Llama 3.3 70B 4bit LM Studio = 11.8 tok/s; 8bit = 6.5; Q8_0 llama.cpp = 4.5 gen / 58 prompt (36k ctx). Independent MLX tests (blog.imseankim.com, corroborated in search) report ~18 tok/s llama.cpp and ~20 tok/s MLX for Llama 3.1 70B Q4, up to 20-28 with MLX at short context. Use ~12 tok/s (llama.cpp/LM Studio Q4) as conservative, ~20 tok/s (MLX Q4) as optimistic. M4 Max bandwidth 410-546 GB/s (40-core = 546). 70B Q4 ~= 40-43GB, fits only 64GB+ configs.

datapoints.value_text: Qwen3 32B Q4_K_M, LM Studio = 11.7 tok/s (measured, 10k ctx); MLX 4-bit dense 32B est. ~18-20 tok/s

datapoints.notes: siliconscore measured: Qwen3 32B Q4_K-Medium via LM Studio = 11.7 tok/s at 10k context. That is llama.cpp-backend; MLX typically 1.3-1.8x faster on Apple Silicon so MLX dense 32B ~18-20 tok/s. Do NOT confuse with MoE Qwen3.5/Qwen3-30B-A3B (3B active) which hits 100+ tok/s. Dense 32B Q4 ~18-20GB memory. Prompt-processing not reported for this row.

datapoints.value_text: MLX Python 4-bit = 126-132 tok/s; MLX HTTP server = 84-108; llama.cpp Q4_K_XL = 70-72; Ollama Q4_K_M = 42-48. ~20GB RAM at 4-bit.

Short prompt (FizzBuzz) so prompt/prefill deliberately minimized/not reported. Best clean primary source for the MLX>llama.cpp>Ollama ordering.

datapoints.label: Framework speedup on Apple Silicon: MLX vs llama.cpp vs Ollama (generation)
datapoints.value_text: MLX ~1.5x faster than llama.cpp and ~2.5-2.7x faster than Ollama for token generation on the same M4 Max (measured on Qwen3.5 35B-A3B: MLX 132 vs llama.cpp 72 vs Ollama 48 tok/s). Smaller (<14B) models can see 1.2-1.9x MLX-over-llama.cpp.
datapoints.source_name: Ante Kapetanovic — Qwen3.5 35B Apple Silicon benchmark
datapoints.notes: Use this multiplier to convert between framework figures. Most 'headline' Apple Silicon numbers are MLX (fastest); Ollama/LM Studio (llama.cpp Metal) numbers run materially lower. HTTP-server MLX adds ~20% overhead vs direct Python API. Choose framework consistently when modeling throughput/revenue.

datapoints.label: Unified-memory footprint at 4-bit (Q4) for each model class
datapoints.value_text: 8B Q4 ~4.5-5 GB (needs 16GB Mac); dense 32B Q4 ~18-20 GB (needs 32GB, comfortably 36-48GB); 70B Q4 ~40-43 GB (needs 64GB+; will OOM on 48GB). Add KV-cache/context on top (grows with context length).
datapoints.source_name: heyuan110 benchmark + siliconscore + Ante Kapetanovic (cross-corroborated)
datapoints.notes: Weights-only Q4 footprints, corroborated across sources: 70B Q4 = ~42GB (OOM'd on M4 Pro mini 48GB in the heyuan110 test); dense 32B Q4 ~18-20GB (Ante K. reports Qwen 35B-A3B MoE ~20GB); 8B Q4 ~4.5-5GB. Long context adds several GB of KV cache. Rule of thumb: usable model size ~= (unified RAM - 8-12GB OS/overhead).

datapoints.label: Long-context generation slowdown on Apple Silicon (single stream)
datapoints.value_text: Up to ~10x slower generation with a large (40-50k token) context loaded vs a near-empty context; all short-prompt tok/s figures above are best-case ceilings.
datapoints.source_name: someoddcodeguy / community caveat (surfaced via search of dev.to M3 Ultra tests)
datapoints.notes: CRITICAL conditions caveat for a revenue model: nearly every headline tok/s here uses a SHORT prompt (e.g. 'Explain daylight savings', FizzBuzz), which maximizes generation rate. With a 40-50k-token document in context, measured generation was reported ~10x slower on M3 Ultra. Real buyer workloads with long prompts/RAG will see substantially lower sustained tok/s than the single-stream short-prompt ceilings. Prefill also dominates latency at long context. Magnitude is anecdotal (hence low confidence) but the directional effect is well established.

datapoints.label: Strix Halo — backend selection (Vulkan vs ROCm/HIP) impact on throughput
datapoints.value_text: HIP/ROCm wins prefill on dense models; Vulkan often wins decode. Vulkan degrades past ~4K ctx; ROCm+FlashAttention stays flat past 8K.
datapoints.notes: Condition-dependent: optimal backend differs between prefill and decode and by context length. Vulkan is the everyday path (fastest decode at short ctx) but degrades noticeably past ~4K tokens; switch to ROCm/HIP with Flash Attention for long-context (flat past 8K). AMD's own marketing uses LM Studio (0.3.11) tokens/sec + TTFT comparisons. NPU (50 TOPS XDNA2) is largely unused for general LLM inference as of 2026 — iGPU (Radeon 8060S, 40 CU) is faster.

datapoints.label: Plausible capacity factor for a home GPU inference node (% of hours serving paid work)
datapoints.value_text: ~5-35% of wall-clock hours; ~15% central estimate for a single residential node
datapoints.source_name: Synthesized bound from Akash (~50-70% network-wide, datacenter-grade), io.net (~2% active), Salad/Render idle-only models, Vast.ai (80% marketing best-case vs idle-consumer reality)
datapoints.notes: DERIVED bound, not a single published figure - flagged low confidence. Reasoning: (1) Even the best-run decentralized DATACENTER network (Akash) tops out ~50-70% and that is an aggregate over pooled, reliable capacity - a ceiling, not a home-node baseline. (2) Consumer/home-hardware networks (io.net ~2% active, Salad/Render explicitly idle-only) realize far less paid time per node because of reliability filtering, buyer preference for verified hosts, residential downtime (gaming, sleep, power/network drops), and dynamic-NAT reachability. (3) Vast.ai's own 80% is an explicit best-case marketing assumption for a well-run verified rig, and its guidance says below ~60% renting beats owning. (4) Demand is bursty and concentrates on trusted/high-density hosts, so a new single residential node captures little. A due-diligence revenue model should use ~10-20% as the base case, stress-test down to ~5%, and treat >35% as optimistic requiring reserved/committed contracts and verified-host reliability. Note this is the DUTY-CYCLE (hours serving), distinct from within-request SM utilization (~19-40%) which further discounts effective throughput/energy-billing.
